title: The 4% Rule: Does It Still Work for U.S. Retirees Today?
description: Re-evaluating the Bengen Rule in an era of lower bond yields and longer lives.
content:
The '4% Rule' is the bedrock of retirement planning. Created by Bill Bengen in 1994, it states that you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio in the first year of retirement, adjust that dollar amount for inflation annually, and have a high probability of not running out of money for 30 years. Recently, critics have argued that lower bond yields and longer life expectancies make 4% too risky. This guide examines the modern data to see if the rule still holds up.

Key Takeaways

  • The Original Math: Based on a 50/50 Stock/Bond portfolio from 1926-1976. It survived the Great Depression and the 1970s stagflation.
  • The 'Safe' Update: For early retirees (40+ year horizon), many experts suggest lowering the rate to 3.25% - 3.5%. This accounts for the longer timeframe.
  • Flexibility Saves: The 4% rule assumes you are a robot who never cuts spending. If you are willing to skip an inflation adjustment during a market crash, the success rate jumps back to near 100%.
  • Asset Allocation: You need stocks. A portfolio of 100% bonds fails the 4% rule because it cannot keep up with inflation. You need at least 50% equities.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 4% rule is specific to the US market, which has been an exceptional performer. Applying it to European or Japanese markets often results in failure. Betting on 4% is betting on the continued resilience of the American economy.

Stress Testing 4%

Does it survive modern valuations?

The Risk: Sequence of Returns

If the market drops 20% the year you retire, and you keep withdrawing 4% of the original balance, you deplete the principal too fast.
Example: $1M Portfolio. Withdraw $40k. Market drops to $800k.
Year 2: You withdraw $41k (inflation). That is now 5.1% of your remaining portfolio. The spiral begins.

The Fix: Variable Withdrawals

Instead of a fixed inflation adjustment, use a 'Guardrails' approach.

  • Good Year: Increase spending by inflation.
  • Bad Year: Freeze spending (no inflation raise) OR cut spending by 10%.

This small behavioral change makes the plan bulletproof.

The Bond Problem

Bengen's data had bonds yielding 5%. Recently, bonds yielded 1%. Today they yield 4-5%. The return of yield makes the 4% rule viable again.

Choosing Your Rate

  1. Standard Retiree (Age 65): 4.0% to 4.5% is safe. You have a shorter horizon (25 years) and Social Security floor.
  2. Early Retiree (Age 50): 3.5% is safe. You have a 45-year horizon.
  3. FIRE (Age 35): 3.0% - 3.25% is safe. You need the money to last forever.
  4. The 'Cash Buffer' Overlay: Keep 2 years of spending in cash. If the market crashes, live on cash. Don't sell stocks. This allows the 4% rule to work without sequence risk.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does it include taxes?

Yes. The $40k withdrawal must cover your taxes. If you need $40k net, you might need to withdraw $45k gross. Plan accordingly.

Is it 4% of the starting balance or current balance?

Original Rule: 4% of Starting balance, adjusted for inflation.
Alternative Rule: 4% of Current balance. (This makes income volatile but guarantees you never run out).

What if I run out?

You will see it coming years in advance. You adjust. You cut spending or get a part-time job at 75. It is rarely a sudden cliff.
